Felipe gave me homework from the podcast to determine what is the tank top level for the diesel export ban scenarios. I took one step further and make a detailed mass balance brief on it, using my experience as a refinery scheduler.

1⃣Depending on how the diesel export ban/quota is framed, Sparta sees the US CDU run cuts could be as low as zero on a blanket ban of 30 days to 17% based on a 90-day export ban.

2⃣This is calculated basis diesel first drawing stocks sharply to exploit the window before the actual export ban date, then running till diesel tank top level.

3⃣There is further reprieve from utilizing mogas storage tanks as well for which there is low risk of contamination in modern tanks.

United States considers limits on diesel exports

The United States is exploring options to prohibit or at least limit diesel exports after domestic prices climbed to a near-record in real terms and stocks remain at the lowest for more than four decades despite record refinery production. 

The United States is the world’s largest exporter of diesel, accounting for about one-fifth of traded supply, so any restrictions would significantly disrupt markets overseas and push up prices, especially in Europe and Latin America. 

The American Petroleum Institute (API) and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers (AFPM), the top trade associations for the oil and gas industry, have expressed strong opposition to a ban on diesel exports.  

Until recently, the U.S. federal government had also rejected proposals to ban or restrict diesel exports as counterproductive ...

Commodity weekly: Macro pressure meets supply tightness

Surging US bond yields and a stronger dollar tested commodities this week, but physical tightness continued to provide a powerful counterweight.

We look at gold’s resilience despite rising real yields, crude oil’s persistent physical stress, diverging US and European gas prices, copper’s tight China fundamentals and the surge in soybean meal.

Despite the tougher macro backdrop, the Bloomberg Commodity Total Return Index remains up around 36% year-to-date. https://t.co/mHG4kYgdZQ via @saxobank

In today's SMC #Podcast I join @johnjhardy to give a run through the outlook for crude oil as we face a key week ahead, given Iran's bid for a 7-day negotiation window with the US. Also in focus  natural gas, the El Niño status and impacts and gold. Elsewhere, a run through the macro and rates and the week ahead, together with interesting single stocks stories driving the market action yesterday https://t.co/gdRVJjQ8F4 via @saxobank

#Commodities (Friday am comment)

BCOM. The Bloomberg Commodity Index is heading for its first, albeit modest, weekly loss in four weeks, down 0.8% and trimming its year-to-date gain to 36%. A stronger dollar and surging bond yields weighed on sentiment across markets, particularly precious metals, while geopolitical risks ebbed and flowed, leaving the energy sector lower overall. Diesel, EU gas and silver are the three biggest weekly losers, while gains are led by US natural gas, cocoa and sugar.

Oil. Brent trades near unchanged on the week at around USD 105.4, having moved within a range of more than USD 10 amid a steady flow of mixed supply and geopolitical developments from the Middle East. The latest focus is on US and Iranian negotiators exploring a phased deal that could see Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz if certain conditions are met. Meanwhile, the prospect of a Trump-backed US diesel export ban sent fuel prices sharply higher earlier in the week before they eased as the industry warned that any short-term reduction in domestic prices could prove fleeting - and potentially be followed by higher costs - as rising US fuel inventories prompt producers and refiners to cut output.

Metals. Gold is down around 3% and silver 5% on the week as investment metals faced a bond-market stress test, with surging Treasury yields supporting a stronger dollar and raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets. Despite these macro headwinds, bullion has remained relatively rangebound over the past month, with traders monitoring support around USD 4,235 and resistance currently near USD 4,400.

Natural gas. Despite a midweek surge, Europe's TTF benchmark is heading for a weekly loss of around 6.5%, trading near EUR 73/MWh (USD 24.30/MMBtu), amid signs that more LNG cargoes have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz. In contrast, the US Henry Hub contract has surged almost 9% after a major pipeline disruption helped trigger a short squeeze as traders reduced sizeable bearish positions. From a low of USD 2.82/MMBBtu on Tuesday, the front-month contract briefly touched USD 3.30 on Thursday before easing back towards USD 3.20.
